blocks.x: Can we get your name now?
You don't know my name.
I don't know your real full name. I don't know what J is for. Joseph. Joseph, okay.

So, what is your real name? My last name is Pecoraro, but I cut it down to Pecoraro. You just called yourself Santa Pecoraro? Yes, and it's a funny thing, then it was about 19, oh, let me see, 19, 20, around 20, Johnny Vittroy started calling me Peck instead of Pecoraro, see? And then when I went to Chicago, they used to make my check out, Peck Pecoraro instead of going to be a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit. So, I stayed in Chicago 15 years, and when I went to California, everybody called me Peck, you know, they knew me from playing the theater there. Am I talking over the telephone? It's working fine. Yeah. So, then I got out there, and, well, I was out in California for about 12 years, and I came back to New Orleans. My mother got crippled, that's why I got back to New Orleans. But my Dave Rose and a bunch of musicians that I worked with in California, they see my picture out there, it says, Santo. They said, well, that's Peck, that's not Santo. I said, where the hell did he get that name? So, Dave looked in the front door, I said, hey, Dave, come in, see? He says, why the hell did you change the name to Santo? See, he says, I said, you're right, everybody, but I said, down in New Orleans, everybody knows me, you know, Santo. So, I just kept the name Santo.
How did your nephew get that name?
Frankie Mann?
No, no, no, Santo Pecoraro, that's your nephew, isn't he?
Oh, that's my dad's brother's son, he says. Yeah, and he was named? Same thing, Santo Pecoraro.
How old is he?
Huh? How old is he? He's about, almost my age, he's about 68, I think.

Oh, I better tell my name and you tell your name so that the- Oh, I said they're gone. Yeah, my name's Dick Allen, anybody that listens to it then will know who's- What's your voice? Which voice is which. Okay. Oh, do you mind my asking your age? No, I'm 70 years old.
You're 70 years old? Born in 1902. What's your birthday?
March the 31st.
March the 31st.
And where were you born? Right in New Orleans.
What part? Oh, in Dauphine, 600 block Dauphine Street.
Oh.
Yeah, just three blocks from the famous-
Did you know Tony Perrini when you were a kid?

Oh sure, we went to school together and we started together. We played an Italian band at St. Mary's Church, you know? Oh yeah. They had an Italian band that used to rehearse in the backyard, had a big room there. In fact, when I first started there I played peclone I see, instead of trombone. I didn't like it. It didn't mean nothing. I couldn't, I mean there was no sense. You couldn't play, you played melody, you would just plump, plump, plump, you know?
Yeah, I know.

One of those things. So, my father said, you know they need trombone players. Trombones were scarce. That was the truth. They didn't have many trombones at that time. So, this fellow used to pass my house all the time. My dad knew him. And he said, why don't you teach that boy how to play an instrument. So, he asked me, what would I like to play? I said, trumpet. He said, well you know they need trombone players, why don't you? I'm going to take lessons on trombone. He said, I can give you some lessons. So, he gave me some lessons and all that stuff. So, I got tired. I said, you know, so phasian, I didn't have a horn yet. I said, look, I've been so phasian, you know, that's reading music, timing and all that stuff. I said, I'm getting tired of this. I said, I don't get a horn. I said, let's just forget about it. So, he told my dad, he went up there and he said, you know something? If you don't give that boy a horn, he's going to quit. He's going to forget about it. So, the next day he says, okay, go ahead and buy him a horn. So, the horn cost nine hours. At that time the horn was cheap. I mean, for eighteen, nineteen or something like that. Bought it for nine hours. And I started playing on it for good horn. And then I started practicing in New York. And would you believe, Vic, that I got offered a co-player of the band? While you were practicing? Practicing. I just bought the horn. See, I was in New York and started practicing. So, the guy knocked on the door. My mother went to the door. And the father said, I speak to that trombone player. She said, well, they're Italian people. Well, that's my son. I said, well, can I talk to him? She said, yeah. So, she called me. So, this father says, was that you playing trombone back there? I said, yeah, I just bought the horn. I said, I'm practicing. I get something out of it. He said, well, who is playing besides you? I said, no, I didn't play myself. I'm practicing. He said, you mean you just bought a horn and you blow a horn like that? I said, I don't know. I just, you know, got the idea. Well, he told me what to do, you know, how to blow it and all that stuff. So, would you believe I went to work for ballet, like the fight, the playlist house and all that stuff, and Dan Hughes, you know?
That's a one-eyed trumpet? Yeah. That's right.

So, when I went to work there, who was playing padcom with Dan Hughes was George and Brunus. Oh, yeah. So, we used to play the fight and all that, like the jungle, the arena, you know what I mean? Used to be the Tulane arena. Used to be the Tulane arena. So, all these musicians. Well, we used to ballet-hoo all day long. And, uh, time to get in the fight. Well, you'd have about 40 musicians with the trombones for fitting in the, you know, getting in the band just to get in the fight, to see the fight, see? So, I finally went there for, oh, for about a year or something like that. Then I went with the Triangle Band, which was about playing with Sato Majada, the other thing again?
Yeah. Yeah.
That used to be with the police band. Yeah, that's right. You read Majada's brother. Yeah, that's right. So...
He died, didn't he? Yeah, he died. Yeah. Yeah. So then I played with him quite a while.

But, uh, we used to, uh, bounty-hoo on Dauphin Street. So, Joe Fulco called me on the side. He says, hey boy, I had to give you a job. I said, what? He says, to play vaudeville. I said, well, I'm not that good. I said, you know, I can't read music that good to play vaudeville, see? He says, I'll teach you. Yeah, well, Sidney Wilson, I don't know if you know the piano player Sidney Wilson? No, I don't know him. He was a trombone player too. Leo Brookhoven, Trappertone. So those two guys really helped me, you know, how to read and all that stuff. And, uh, I played at theater for quite a while. Then I got more damn offers to go to New York, you know, like Lanning, and all these guys sent me telegrams, offered me a lot of money to leave there. We had all these vaudeville entertainers like a, see, they played a circuit, see, and they said, man, you want to hear a trombone play? I'm bragging about myself there. He says, go into New Orleans. I said, I want to hear a kid that plays trombone, he plays good. But I used to stand up and play solos all the time. You know, like I said, at that time I didn't have no competition. They had just about four or five cromwell players that, you know, I knew how to play around here.
Yeah, I guess Andy Edwards had left. I think, though.
Yeah, well, he left, let's see, oh, I think about two years after I went to the Palace Theater.
Was Emil Christian playing trombone then or trumpet?
Who was that?
Emil Christian. He was playing trombone.
Well, Emil plays trombone, plays bass. Yeah, but at that time, was he playing trombone?
He didn't know trombone.
He didn't know he had a brother that played trumpet, a good trumpet boy. I had forgotten his name. Frank. Frank, yeah. See, he knows them all. Let's stop a second and see if he's recording all right.
Yeah, let's see. I wanted to ask you some more if we can get back. Who was your first teacher?
I'm going to forget his name.
Vigory.
Vigory? Vigory, yeah. You don't remember his first name? No, I never did. I don't know if it was John.
I'm sure we can find it out one more time. I imagine Louis Panzeri will know, because he knows all the teachers. You know Louis.
That's the only name I remember. Yeah.
And what about the Italian band? Who else was in that? Tony Perrani and...
Oh, Manuel Alexander. You remember? Yeah, sure. Well... Do you remember...
Do you remember... Fanazzi? Mario Fanazzi? Yeah, yeah.
Was he there then?
He was there then. He was there then. I know his son too. Well, uh...
The guys that played in that band... Tony Perrani and I was the only one that got to be known, you know, to go out of town. Yeah.
I'm trying to think of the guys from the French Quarter then. Who was that? Johnny Lala was around? Was he with you to? Well, Johnny Lala didn't play with the Italian band, no.
He played with just like Valley Hoon, dances and all that stuff. Yeah. He played with Schilling band for a long time.
And would you believe...

Well, he was... The guy was supposed to go with what's called Dixieland Band, to New York, see. But he wouldn't go because he had a meat market with his dad. And so he says, no, I can make more money here. But he was a better trumpet player than Nick, you know. I mean, he moved the band. That's what they said. So... Like, see, Johnny Lala was known, uh... Oh, man. They must have had a lot of good musicians, you know, probably. Well, all the Brunner's boys played good. That's the boy that I work with all the time. Jack Lane, you know. You heard of Jack Lane. Pansy Lane, Jack Lane's son. But like I said, there's Italian band.
Just Tony Fernand and I that came out of the band. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. 50 piece band. We used to play all these parades, you know. And we used to wear those Italian uniforms. I mean, it was really Italian band though. I've seen pictures of the old ones,
you know. Oh you didn't? I think like some parade, like Contessa Antiglia, would be posed in front of the church. And they'd all line up in front of the church.

And we used to play the Italian all the time. But I didn't stay too long with the Italian band, because I started playing with these Dixieland bands. And then when I quit playing with the Dixieland, I went to play vaudeville. And then I went to Chicago with this B. Palmer, the shimmy shaker that came from Chicago. She took Rapport, Emmett Hardy, you know those boys. Frisco, Johnny Frisco. And we played vaudeville. And in fact, that's where the New Orleans Rhythm Kings started. She named, that's what she named the band, B. Palmer and her New Orleans Rhythm Kings.
I never knew that.
Yes sir.
That's how they got their name?
No. What did you say?
That's how they got their name?
And so they took their name from her, you see?
Yeah. And she already had Rapp and Emmett Hardy?
Hardy, myself and Frisco. Her husband was the piano player, Al Segal. And that's all in five pieces.
Where was Johnny Frisco from?
From here. He just died about a couple of years ago. I never knew him. I never knew him. Well, he played with Johnny Long with the Shillen Band for all time. He was raised for a damn good drummer.
Yeah. But, well, did you ever play at the Orpheum?
No, I never did. The Palace Theater. I played Liberty with Max Finks. Do you remember? You heard Max Finks?
I heard of him. I never knew him. He was before I ever got here.

He was terrific. Good showman and all that stuff. But, like I say, I went to Chicago and I came back to New Orleans. I went back to the Palace. But I just wanted to go back to, you know, out of town, so I went back to Chicago. So, I went back there and I played the dance hall, like the Mary Garden. That was a big deal. And, who happened to have two dance halls ones? It was like a T. And, uh, Paul Moreas and George Abrunas, they played with the other band, Ben Pollack, you know, and all that stuff. That's where that band started out. This was at the Mary Garden. Mary Garden, yeah. That's on an art sign. I think it was on Crawford. So, I played a few night club, like the Green Mill, that was where the Tiberi Theater is now, up on, have you been in Chicago? Not in a long time. Well, you know where the Tiberi Theater is now, up on, and I think. I remember it kind of vaguely. You know where Lawrence Avenue.
I know where the Drake Hotel is. That's about all I can remember now. It's been so many years ago. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

And then, uh, I started playing Waterville. Went back to Waterville. I played with the Chicago Theater with a 50-piece band, you know, in the pit. And then, uh, we had stage presentation on stage after we got finished playing the pit band. That was a 25-piece band on the stage. So, I stayed there quite a while, but a little over 10 years. And then, uh, I played with Benny, uh, Benny Miroff. You heard of Benny Miroff?
Yeah. I heard his records, anyway. Huh?

He made some records with Wild Bill, you know. Yeah, Wild Bill did. He played with the band. That's right. Maury Stein, the writer on Hollywood, was writing a lot of tunes, you know. He writes a lot of tunes.
Uh-huh. Before I forget it, how did George Bernays get his first trombone?

He bought, he was supposed to buy my trombone for nine bucks. Yeah. And every time I see him, I say, when are you going to give me my nine bucks? He says, would you believe I got that same trombone and I ain't going to give you the nine dollars? He still got you? Yeah. That's the first horn you ever? Yeah. He tells me that all the time. I says, uh, I can't curse. I don't want to curse. Yeah. I say, hey boy, I says, when are you going to give me my nine dollars? I ain't going to give you nine dollars. I ain't going to give you a horn back. I still got your horn. Yeah. I said, good. That's pretty good. I didn't care if we could charge in. I'm a pretty good friend, you know. Yeah. You know, I didn't know him when he came in town last month. Yeah. Came at the famous door, sat at the bar.
You didn't know him? You look so different?

He's changed so much and he kept waving at me and I said, howdy, howdy, that's it. And, uh, when I got off the stand, he said, you know who's sitting by the bar? That's George Apprentice. So he left, see, before
I had time to talk to him. God. I didn't get to talk to him either. He's had some operations and

everything. Yeah. Well, George is only a jobbing lately, you know. You see, George never played with bands like I did, you know. He played with Ted Lewis, you know, one of those things. But at that time, Dick, you didn't have to know how to read music or nothing. They were fakers, see. In fact, a lot of good jazz musicians, or good musicians, they can't read music. But still, they can't get a job with big bands because they have to read the charts. Well, he couldn't play shows. You see, you can't play shows or nothing like that. Well, see, that's what happened. And I love Pete Fountain. That's what happened with Lawrence Welch, see. He couldn't sit in the band and read the charts, see. So, that's... And Lawrence Welch said, look, I'm a... I got five, six saxophone players. They'll teach you how to play, read music. So he didn't want it that way. So he made a reputation just with that one tune. With Lawrence Welch, what was that? Every week? Yeah. Was it every night? No. It's every week, huh? Every week? Every once a week he would come. I don't know. Well, anyhow, then he made his reputation.

I gave it up. I had to quit. Yeah. What about playing a silent movie? What would that be like? Would you have to read much to do that? Oh. What a new movie would come up like? How would you play it? How did you know what to do?

Well, I never did play silent. Oh, you never did? No. I never did. I played... The only thing I played... around 1936 when I... first movie I made with Bing Crosby, rhythm on the river. You know, where they can see you and they can hear you play.
Oh, you were in that? With Wingy? Yeah.
Yeah, I got the picture. I've never seen it.
No. I've heard the record, you know, that Wingy.

What's the name of the movie? Uh, uh, Rhythm on the River. It's a good tune. It's a good tune, sure. Uh, Larry Crosby was supposed to send me the music and I never did get it, so... I might have it. Yeah? Call me when I get back to work. Yeah. And I'll look it up right there for you. Yeah, all right.
I've got it by Wingy. And I... You did, yeah. You know the record? I think it's on the back of I think, well, ain't it a shame about name or something like that, you know?
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
That's good. Good numbers. Well, suppose a new act would come in. How would you play that? Would you have to rehearse with... Oh, yeah.
All these shows you rehearse. You're talking about...
Vaudeville. Like at the Palace.
Yeah, well, they have a two-hour rehearsal and you got about six or seven acts and everybody just tells you what they want, how the music... You run over maybe once and that's it.
Mm-hmm.

But, uh, you have to be a sight reader, you know what I mean? Oh, yeah. Yeah. And at that time, uh, you know, you used to get some crazy music, like, uh, big overtures and all that stuff. You play, you see?
Did you ever have to get up on the stage or put on a costume or anything you said?

No, no. Well, you're not in the Palace. Yeah. Where would you put on a costume? When I went to Chicago, when I played in Chicago, we used to wear costumes, all kinds of costumes. Chinese outfits, Mexican outfits.
For different acts then? Yeah, I see. No, it just...
The show that would come in, you know, they put costumes.
Depends on what kind of show it was. Would you be in the pit in the costume or on the stage?
On the stage.
That'd make you get up on the stage?

Yeah. Oh, in the pit you rest just like you rest every day. But that was a good experience. I'll tell you, the best experience I ever had in music, when I played Chicago Theatre, was two trombones, three trumpets, and all about 25 fiddle players, and all that stuff. And it was beautiful to play that music. And when you get on the stage, you got something, it's like the contrast, you know? Something different, see? You're playing two types of music. Yeah, see? And I'll tell you, Dick, when I played at the Chicago Theatre, they had some fine musicians from Europe there. I think over half of the band, orchestra, let's say orchestra, was from Europe, from all over, Russia, Finland.
And I'm a band leader. And I'm a band leader.

I was working at the Capitol Theatre in Chicago. Oakland Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church Church give two weeks notice. He said, how much money you want? Well I said, I make him pretty good at the Capitol Theater with Roy Eldridge. He was a band leader and MC.
That's not the trumpet player.

No, piano player played piano. Roy Eldridge. Yeah, this fellow. He had a band in Detroit for a long time, I had the theater there too. So I went there and this fellow says, I'll tell you, I'll give you 200, he said I paid a musician, the band, $125, $150. I said, oh, then you don't want me. He says, well, no, he said, I want you to give me the price. So I told him, $250. He said, well that's a lot of money. He said, I'll give you $250. I said, well, don't worry about it. I said, I have a job. I'll go, you know. How much were you making on the other job? I said, I'll give you $200. So I asked him $250 more to leave there. So he said, sign these papers. So I signed this year, contract. So after I got finished signing the contract, he says, you know something, if you'd have asked me for $500, you could have got it.
Good Lord. You must have been making some money at that place then.

Why? I could have bumped my head. You see, I'm a young kid, you don't know, you know what they, well, you see, I was raided in Chicago. Yeah. You understand? Tommy Dawson was never heard of yet and all that stuff. But then just like New Orleans, I was raided here. Would you believe I got more money than all the musicians? Oh yeah. Instead of the lead item. I always got $25 or $50. So when I was working at the Palace Theater, you don't remember the Little Club, like before your time I think.
I heard of it that time.

Yeah, it was on Common and Drive. Tony DiNopolis had a place there. So they had a band from Scranton, Pennsylvania. Yeah, another one you're talking about. Yeah, sure. So Billy Lustig. So he came to the Palace and he says, Joe, Tony DiNopolis told him to come here and ask you if you want to take this job after you get off the theater. I said, yeah, how much you pay? He said, well I'll give you $100 and a quarter. I said, what? $100 and a quarter? I said, the trombone player had to go home and get operated. I said, I'll tell you what I'll do. I'll take what you give the other trombone player. He said, well I can't give you that. I said, well forget about it. So he said, well I'm sorry. I said, well I'm sorry. I said, okay, that's all right. So we went back and Tony DiNopolis says, did you hire Santa? He says, he wants too much money. He said, well how much do you want to pay him? He said, well how much do you want to pay him? He said, well how much do you want to pay him? the doctor says, did you hire a Santa? He says, he wants too much money. He said, well how much you want to pay him? He said, I want to, he said, well how much you gave the other trombone player? He said, well give him the same, give him the same thing, see. So he came back and he said, well good job, I got $200. And I was making $75 at the Powell Street, the scale was $45, I was making $75. And you know when I said 19, 20, 21, 22. That's a lot of money. No tax. So then I went to Chicago with Billy Lustig and I couldn't get there. I had to give two weeks notice for Keir to see before I could get to Chicago. So he used Tommy Darcy on the trombone. So I got there, Tommy Darcy played and I played. And he used to say, Barney says, you get a big tone on the trombone. I said, yes, but you get a pretty tone on it. He said, yeah, but my tone ain't bigger than yours, you know, one of those things. So I used to love to hear him play because he played so beautiful. Then the trumpet player, you heard of Johnny Bystorfer?
Yeah, I knew him.

Yeah, you knew him. All right. Johnny Bystorfer got sick for about three weeks. So Tommy takes the trumpet and plays the big show. I can believe it. A beautiful trumpet. Oh man. I said, how in the hell can you play trumpet and take the trumpet? He used to like the trombones. He wanted to play trombone. But he used to play that show, cut that show like that.
He sounded like Joe Olive on trumpet to me. Some of the records. He sounded like Joe Olive on trumpet. No. Somebody could play Rattie on trumpet.

No, he sounded like Harry James or Spivak or something like that. Oh, he had a beautiful tone. Everything, numb pressure and all that. Tommy played beautiful. Look at it. But he had to get on that trombone. But him and I, and he used to practice in the hotel room. Gee, nine o'clock in the morning. We'd go home about four o'clock in the morning. Get up at nine o'clock and practice with records and all that stuff. We got to be pretty good friends. Well, you know who bought Jack Teagarden first trombone? Me. You did? Jack Teagarden was working at, what's up? I'm not Lake Charles, St. Charles, Louisiana. What's that little town? Lake Charles. No, not Lake Charles. It's close by here.
How far is it? Up the river?
Yeah, it's past like...
St. Charles Parish?
St. Charles, I think they had an oil field or somewhere there. Yeah. I don't know.
I can look it up.

So, Jack used to come at the palace. Mm-hmm. So, he'd come backstage and says, I'm Jack Teagarden. He says, I'd like to meet you, see. I'm going to play a trombone. He says, I want to play trombone. He says, would you do me a favor? He says, would you go with me? I went to oil and I got a trombone with him.
Mm-hmm.

He took off that money and we went to get a trombone. You know when Jack Teagarden, when he died here? Yeah. He checked in Prince County and he threw his grip there in the lobby, told the bar to bring it up and came to the famous door. He played the dream room and every cell used to come at the famous door to see me. That's how close we were.
And what was he playing when he came here? He looked at the dream room. No, no, no. Before when he was a kid. No, he wasn't going to play music. Oh, he was playing.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
We've got the second reel on now Santa.
We were talking about, oh, let me see, I had something I wanted to ask you. All right. How much did they pay at Toros?
Uh, downtown? Yeah. I think the salary was around $35 a week, $30, something like that.
Well, that was good money for a place like that.
Oh, yeah, well, I played the Groomall Hotel, at Roosevelt Hotel now, with Johnny Deidre, I only got $20. I think it was from $10.30 to $1, $20 a week. But we made tips. We had made with.
This is the third reel, Santa. Yeah. We're set, we're going.
I was going to ask you when the trombone started playing lead. When did they ever begin doing that?

Trombone never played lead. They played just like maybe six bars, eight bars or something like that, you know, arrangement, orchestration or something like that, or arrangement, they had trombone to play a certain part, you know. But trombone play didn't play it. Now, I noticed all the records you hear or tape on, like in the ballrooms and all that stuff, you hear nothing but trombone leads. You hear nothing but three trombones playing and the trombones taking the leads to the trumpet.
Yeah.
Well. Honestly, I sit in the Amson bar every night and every set almost, I go there and relax and I hear these records and the trombones are taking the melody. Yeah. Right? That's true.
What about, how did you get that name, Mr. Tailgate, I wanted to ask you.

Well, you see, you know the funny thing, I had a club in Baton Rouge, and I named it the Tailgate Club. And two ladies came there and said, could you tell me what you mean by tailgate? I said, alright. I said, you see, when I was a kid, we used to valley-hoo on a wagon, so the trombone probably couldn't get inside the wagon. They had the drums and all that stuff and they didn't have room to slide these slides. Because on the outside had signs on both sides, see, so you didn't have room to slide. So they put you on a tailgate. See, the bass player and the trombones sat on the tailgate. Well, they had plenty of room to slide. That's why it said tailgate trombone. That's what it was.

But who put the name on you? Huh? Who gave you the name, Mr. Tailgate? Well, I don't know how that happened, see. Well, it's been a long time. Oh, yeah, gee. At least 20 years, or more than that. Oh, more than that, yeah.
Twice, 40, 50 years.
Yeah. People said tailgate trombone.

And I think I overheard somebody say that the trombone sits on a tailgate, see. And a lot of people ask me that all the time, we're on a club. Where did you get the name tailgate? So I explained them. You sit on a tailgate when you play. It's the only place you have room. Just like the bass fiddle used to. Boy, that was a hell of a thing. Sometimes you had some bad horses, you know.
Yeah.
It would knock you right out of the wagon, see. It could break your heart. Well, break everything. Breeding your lips and everything. Break your mouth and everything.
Yeah. Did you play while the wagon was moving?
Oh, yeah, sometimes, sure. But we used to go on corners, barns, you know, and play all those corners. Just like you see a lot of these colored bands, let alone all these wagons. Yeah.
And you'd go and play boxing then? Yeah. Would you play between rounds or before?
Yeah, between rounds, yeah.
